meta.title: Who really said "Time heals all wounds"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Cicero — Wikiquote files it under Misattributed. The oldest record is Terence, 163 BC, whose character calls the saying false.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Time heals all wounds'?
meta.ogDescription: Cicero never wrote it, and argued the opposite. Terence recorded the saying in 163 BC; the exact English wording is first found in print in 1910.

answer.label: Not Cicero — a proverb, oldest record by Terence
answer.authorDates: c. 195/185 – c. 159 BC · Roman comic playwright; earliest known to write the saying down
answer.sourceLine: No line matching the saying survives anywhere in Cicero, and in Tusculan Disputations Book III he grants that grief fades with time only to argue that the cure is daily reflection, not elapsed time. The oldest surviving record is Terence’s comedy Heauton Timorumenos (163 BC), where Menedemus quotes it as “that saying which I hear commonly repeated” and then flatly rejects it; the exact English wording came centuries later, from no identifiable author.

source.heading: The oldest record: Terence, 163 BC

docMeta.dd: Act III, scene 1, line 421 — spoken by Menedemus
Henry Thomas Riley, Perseus Digital Library edition

source.excerpt: Assuredly I was either born with a disposition peculiarly suited for misery, or else that saying which I hear commonly repeated, that ‘time assuages human sorrow,’ is false.
trail: Wikiquote’s Cicero page ↗ lists “Time heals all wounds” in its Misattributed section, glossing it “Truly from Terentius, Heautontimorumenos, Act III, scene i.”

The Latin at Perseus confirms the line and its speaker: Menedemus, Heautontimorumenos III.1 ↗ — quod vulgo audio dici, “what I commonly hear said.” The saying was already old when Terence wrote it down.

Cicero took the other side. In Tusculan Disputations III he asks how grief can change if neither its cause nor the mourner has changed, and concludes that the remedy comes “from daily reflecting… and not from the length of time” (§ 74, trans. C. D. Yonge, 1877 ↗).

The exact four-word English form is modern. Phrases.org.uk ↗ locates its earliest printing in H. Rider Haggard’s novel Morning Star (1910), and the passage is there in the Project Gutenberg text ↗: “We quarrelled long ago, did we not… but Time heals all wounds.”
source.excerptNote: The Latin behind it is aut illud falsum est, quod vulgo audio dici, diem adimere aegritudinem hominibus — and quotation books have long lifted the final clause out on its own, translating it as “time heals all wounds.” Read whole, Menedemus is not endorsing the proverb. He is saying his grief over his absent son grows heavier by the day, and that the saying is a lie.

sourceLink.text: Terence, The Self-Tormentor, Act III scene 1 — Perseus Digital Library

source.rightsNote: Every text quoted on this page is out of copyright in the United States. Terence’s Latin is ancient; Henry Thomas Riley’s English rendering and C. D. Yonge’s 1877 Cicero are nineteenth-century; H. Rider Haggard’s Morning Star was published in 1910 — all comfortably before the 1931 threshold. The proverb itself has no identifiable author, so there is no one to hold a right in the four words.

author.name: Terence
author.heading: Terence — who wrote it down, and then disowned it
author.metaLine: c. 195/185 – c. 159 BC · Roman comic playwright, born in Carthage
author.bio: Publius Terentius Afer was brought to Rome as a slave from Carthage, educated in his master’s household, and freed. Between 166 and 160 BC he wrote six comedies, all of which survive complete, most of them adapted from Greek originals by Menander — including Heauton Timorumenos, staged in 163 BC. His plain, conversational Latin made him a school text for centuries, which is precisely why his lines travelled so far from their contexts and were so easily reshelved under grander Roman names. He did not invent the idea that time heals: he set down a saying he already found commonplace, and handed it to a character who insists it is untrue.

copyAttribution: “Time heals all wounds” — not Cicero. It is an anonymous proverb. The oldest surviving record is Terence, Heauton Timorumenos (163 BC), Act III sc. 1, line 421, where the speaker quotes it as a commonplace and calls it false; Cicero in fact argued the opposite in Tusculan Disputations III.74. The exact English wording is earliest located in H. Rider Haggard's Morning Star (1910). Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who it isn't
misattribution.intro: “Time heals all wounds” is a proverb, and proverbs attract famous names the way lightning finds a rod. Cicero is the usual host, but he is not the only bad address on this line.

items.why: Wikiquote’s Cicero page ↗ places the phrase in its Misattributed section and points to Terence instead. The credit is not merely unsupported, it is backwards: in Tusculan Disputations III Cicero holds that a remedy for grief comes “from daily reflecting that there is no real evil in the circumstance for which you grieve, and not from the length of time” (§ 74, trans. C. D. Yonge ↗).

Terence is the oldest source, but crediting him with the sentiment inverts his scene. Menedemus introduces the words as quod vulgo audio dici — what I commonly hear said — and immediately declares the saying false ↗, because his own sorrow grows heavier by the day.

Quote collections often push the thought back to Menander as “time is the healer of all necessary evils.” Phrases.org.uk ↗ cautions that this rests on quotation collections rather than surviving fragments, and notes that some sources credit Diphilus instead. Terence’s play was itself adapted from a Menander original ↗ now too fragmentary to check, so the trail genuinely runs cold.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody coined it. Terence heard it as a commonplace in 163 BC and gave it to a character who calls it a lie; the earliest printing of the exact English wording that phrase historians have located is H. Rider Haggard’s Morning Star of 1910 (Phrases.org.uk ↗), where a Pharaoh offers it to the half-brother he once quarrelled with.

context.heading: Why Cicero is the wrong name in a particularly pointed way
lead: The irony is hard to miss. Cicero is the name pinned to “time heals all wounds,” and Cicero is the ancient writer who most explicitly refused the idea. In Tusculan Disputations Book III he takes the claim apart on its own terms: if the cause of the grief is unchanged and the mourner is unchanged, why should mere elapsed time alter anything? His conclusion is that it does not — the cure is “daily reflecting that there is no real evil in the circumstance for which you grieve,” and not the length of time ↗.

There is a plausible route by which his name got attached anyway. The closest parallel anywhere in the Ciceronian corpus is nullus dolor est, quem non longinquitas temporis minuat ac molliat — there is no grief that length of time does not lessen and soften — and it sits in Epistulae ad Familiares 4.5 ↗. That letter is bound into Cicero’s collected correspondence, but Cicero did not write it: it is Servius Sulpicius Rufus writing to Cicero, consoling him on the death of his daughter. A sentence indexed under “Cicero, Letters” is one careless step from a sentence attributed to Cicero. That last step is our own observation, not a documented chain — but it is exactly the kind of slip this corpus invites.
context.detailsSummary: How the English wording actually formed
detailsBody: The thought is old and diffuse rather than authored. Menedemus already treats it as street wisdom in 163 BC, and Terence’s play was adapted from a lost Menander original ↗, so the saying may well have been Greek before it was Latin. What survives is a proverb already in circulation, not a first utterance.

In English it surfaces first as an image, not a formula. Chaucer’s Pandarus consoles Troilus with “As tyme hem hurt, a tymë doth hem cure” ↗ in Book V of Troilus and Criseyde — time as both the wound and the cure, which is the same idea entirely without the modern phrasing.

The fixed four-word form is recent by comparison. Its earliest located printing is 1910, in Haggard’s Morning Star; the near-variant “time is a great healer” turns up in Percy F. Westerman’s The Rival Submarines in 1913 and in Punch in 1914, according to Phrases.org.uk ↗. Nothing anywhere in that chain runs through Cicero.
context.pull: The one Roman most often credited with the saying is the one who argued against it.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Marcus Tullius Cicero. The saying is an anonymous proverb; Terence is its oldest surviving record (163 BC), not its author — his character quotes it as a commonplace and calls it false.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Marcus Tullius Cicero page lists "Time heals all wounds" (Latin: Diem adimere aegritudinem hominibus) in its Misattributed section, noting it is "Truly from Terentius, Heautontimorumenos, Act III, scene i."
The Latin of Heautontimorumenos Act 3 scene 1 reads "aut illud falsum est, quod vulgo audio / Dici, diem adimere aegritudinem hominibus" and the speaker is Menedemus.

Henry Thomas Riley's English translation of Act 3 scene 1 reads: "Assuredly I was either born with a disposition peculiarly suited for misery, or else that saying which I hear commonly repeated, that 'time assuages human sorrow,' is false."

WIST cites the line as Terence, Heauton Timoroumenos, Act 3, sc. 1, l. 12 (l. 421), Latin "Diem adimere aegritudinem hominibus," with variant English renderings "Time removes distress," "Time heals all wounds," and "Time assuages sorrow."

Wikiquote's Terence page gives "Diem adimere aegritudinem hominibus" — "Time removes distress" — cited to Heauton Timorumenos Act III scene 1, line 12 (421), with the variant translation "Time heals all wounds."

Cicero, Tusculan Disputations Book III § 74, in C. D. Yonge's 1877 translation, reads: "Therefore it is from daily reflecting that there is no real evil in the circumstance for which you grieve, and not from the length of time, that you procure a remedy for your grief."
Epistulae ad Familiares 4.5 is a letter from Servius Sulpicius to Cicero consoling him on his daughter's death, and contains "Nullus dolor est, quem non longinquitas temporis minuat ac molliat."

Phrases.org.uk states the exact phrase "Time heals all wounds" first appears in H. Rider Haggard's 1910 novel Morning Star; cautions that the Menander credit rests on quotation collections rather than surviving fragments (some sources credit Diphilus); and records "time is a great healer" in Percy F. Westerman's The Rival Submarines (1913) and in Punch (1914).

The Project Gutenberg edition of H. Rider Haggard's Morning Star (ebook 2722) contains the sentence: "We quarrelled long ago, did we not, and many years have passed since we met, but Time heals all wounds and--welcome, son of my father." — confirmed by direct text search of the Gutenberg plain-text file.
Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde, Book V, contains the line "As tymë hem hurt, a tymë doth hem cure" in the stanza at lines 5.343-349, spoken by Pandarus to Troilus.

Terence's Heauton Timorumenos was written/produced in 163 BC and was translated wholly or in part from an earlier Greek play by Menander, of which too little survives to judge the extent of the adaptation.

Terence (Publius Terentius Afer), c. 195/185 BC – c. 159 BC, was a Roman comic playwright born in Carthage and brought to Rome as a slave, later freed; he wrote six comedies between 166 and 160 BC, adapted from Greek originals by Menander or Apollodorus of Carystus.
H. Rider Haggard's Morning Star was first published in 1910 by Cassell (UK) and Longmans Green (US).
Quotepark's page for the Cicero attribution of "Time heals all wounds" itself flags the attribution as Misattributed and states "Truly from Terentius, Heautontimorumenos, Act III, scene i."
